items.title: Elizabeth I owned around 80 wigs and 2,000 dresses
items.claim: Elizabeth I's image — the painted face, the wigs — was carefully constructed. How extensive was the wardrobe?

options.text: A handful of ceremonial robes for state occasions only
Inventories at her death (1603) recorded around 2,000 gowns and roughly 80 wigs, with ceruse make-up to mask smallpox scarring from 1562
She refused jewels and dressed plainly throughout her reign

items.reveal:
Elizabeth survived smallpox in October 1562 with scarring on her face and neck. She used ceruse (white lead and vinegar) to whiten her skin — slowly poisonous.

Nicholas Hilliard's 'Treatise Concerning the Arte of Limning' notes that after about 1590 painters were instructed not to show shadow on her face — the 'Mask of Youth' image. The wardrobe was a political instrument: gifts from courtiers carried specific meanings.
items.why: Elizabeth's reign was a sustained exercise in image management. The 'Gloriana' iconography was deliberate state branding, not personal vanity.

items.title: Most Roman emperors died violently
items.claim: Of the 69 Roman emperors from Augustus (27 BCE) to Theodosius I (395 CE), how many died of natural causes?

options.text: Almost all — emperors were generally well-protected
Roughly a third — the rest died by assassination, in battle, by suicide or under suspicious circumstances
All emperors after Nero were murdered

items.reveal:
Joseph Saleh and colleagues (2019) modelled imperial deaths and found violent end rates above 50% for the first 25 years of any reign. The Crisis of the Third Century (235-284) saw around 50 emperors and usurpers in 50 years.

Named assassinations: Caligula (41), Claudius (54, probably poisoned by Agrippina), Domitian (96), Commodus (192), Caracalla (217), Elagabalus (222) and many more. Some died in war (Decius at Abrittus, 251; Valerian captured by the Persians, 260).
items.why: The imperial succession looks orderly from the list of names. Statistically, becoming emperor was one of the most dangerous jobs in the ancient world — which itself shaped imperial policy.

items.title: Thomas Becket was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170

options.text: Becket died of natural causes during a service

Four knights of Henry II — Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy, Richard le Breton — murdered Archbishop Becket in Canterbury Cathedral after Henry's outburst 'Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?'
He was executed for treason after a public trial

items.reveal:
Becket and Henry had clashed for years over the jurisdiction of church courts (Constitutions of Clarendon, 1164). Becket had fled to France, returned in 1170, and excommunicated bishops who had supported Henry. The king's exact words are disputed but the four knights took them as licence.

Becket was canonised in 1173. Henry II did public penance at Canterbury in 1174, walking barefoot and being scourged by monks. The shrine became one of medieval Europe's major pilgrimage sites — the setting of Chaucer's 'Canterbury Tales' (1380s).

Henry VIII destroyed the shrine in 1538 during the Dissolution.
items.why: Church-state conflict was the defining political question of high medieval Europe. Becket's murder dramatised the limits of royal power over the church — and made Canterbury a centre of European devotion for 350 years.
